why: Editing and outlining one's own work vs AI feedback vs AI-drafted content.

options.name: AI for editing, proofreading and outlining one's own work
options.covers: AI may help with editing, proofreading, grammar, outlining, organizing or revising one's own writing. P18 is about treating prose differently from code; this is the permission itself. Evidence: Morehouse, Rutgers, NAU, Ohio State, Oakland, Rowan, Penn State, Rush, NC State.

options.name: AI feedback or critique on one's own work
options.covers: Using AI to get feedback, critique or review of one's own draft, code or solution (not to produce it). From P14, P91 subgroups and NEW labels.

options.name: AI-generated content or code in submitted work
options.covers: Students may submit or use AI-generated code under explicit conditions (small snippets, line or percentage caps, cited, specific projects, or freely).

units.passage: Your recommendations for using these tools will depend on your discipline, pedagogy, and learning objectives, but may include answering simple factual questions, breaking down complex concepts (“explain protein folding to a college student”), checking paper drafts for grammar and readability, or serving as a “Socratic opponent” that raises objections to a submitted piece of argumentation.
units.why: The same sentence recommends "checking paper drafts for grammar and readability"; a writing-support permission (P91), separate from the tutor use.

units.passage: We consider it necessary for faculty to clarify to students whether AI tools that help with editing (e.g., Quillbot, Paraphrase, Grammarly) are permitted and to what extent.
units.why: The report finds it 'necessary for faculty to clarify to students whether AI tools that help with editing (e.g., Quillbot, Paraphrase, Grammarly) are permitted', a rule about the editing-tool category; nearest P91.

units.passage: Use for Editing Only Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools may be used throughout the course to improve your original work but cannot be used to do the initial creation of an assignment.
units.why: Statement 3: AI "may be used throughout the course to improve your original work" is a permission for editing, P91.

units.passage: Forms of writing assistance that utilize artificial intelligence (AI) to proofread a student’s own written work (such as spellcheck or Grammarly) are acceptable. However, tools that rely on generative AI (such as GPT-3, ChatGPT, and Bard) that actually “write” (or generate) text from a prompt are not to be used to generate drafts or written work for any assignment in this course.
units.why: Sample Restrictive Statement Two: AI that proofreads "a student's own written work (such as spellcheck or Grammarly) are acceptable", a permission for editing support: P91 (P100 not chosen since the point is permission for proofreading).
Listed specific usage 'editing (e.g., Grammarly)' as a permissible AI task (P91); instructor, during-work, may.

units.passage: To access just-in-time support at various stages of the learning process: generating or testing out ideas or formulas; summarizing or distilling complex thinking; learning specific genre conventions; checking grammar
units.why: 'checking grammar' and 'learning specific genre conventions' are listed uses of AI for writing support (P91).

units.passage: In this course, it is permitted to use Generative AI chat services such as ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and Claude as a tool to aid in your understanding of content, to develop ideas, and edit drafts of your work.
units.why: The same sentence permits AI to "edit drafts of your work", an editing and writing-support permission, P91.

units.passage: UG 1: Polish, with disclosure. You may use AI to check and correct the grammar, vocabulary, spelling, and mechanics of text you have already written. AI may not generate, rewrite, or restructure your content.
units.why: UG 1 says "AI may not generate, rewrite, or restructure your content", a limit on producing submitted text (P19).
